system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
You were admitted to the hospital on February 3, 2020, and discharged on May 9, 2020, after staying for 3 months, 6 days, and 7 hours. You were referred to us because you had a cough for 4 weeks that was dry, meaning no phlegm came out, along with night sweats. You also mentioned having a fever three days before admission, which you didn't measure, and difficulty breathing (dyspnea). One day before admission, you suddenly felt pain in the right side of your chest (right hemithorax) that spread to your right neck area (right cervical region), and your difficulty breathing got much worse. You said you didn't cough up any blood. You also mentioned being in prison for about 3 years, and for 6 years you had no symptoms. About a month ago, you lost about 8 kg of weight. You didn't report any changes in your urine or bowel movements (motions).

When you were examined, your general condition was regular. You were a bit pale, hydrated, not blue (acyanotic), not yellow (anicteric), and fully conscious and aware. Your heart sounds were normal, with a rate of 85 beats per minute. When we listened to your lungs, the left lung sounded normal, but the right lung had no breath sounds, and your chest expansion was uneven. Your oxygen saturation was 98%. Your abdomen was flat, soft, and had normal bowel sounds. Your arms and legs had no swelling (edema) or signs of blood clots. Your surgical wound was in good condition and dry, with stitches that were not open.

Tests on your sputum (phlegm) collected on March 2, 2020, showed that you had tuberculosis (TB) that was sensitive to common medicines like rifampin and isoniazid. This means the medicines should work well. The test also showed many TB bacteria (mycobacteria bacilloscopy) in your sputum.

Your main problem was sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis (TB in the lungs), diagnosed in 2019, with treatment starting on February 7, 2020, and ending on April 7, 2020. You had several complications because of the TB. On February 3, 2020, you developed a spontaneous pneumothorax (a collapsed lung where air leaks into the space around the lung) on your right side, which needed a chest drain (a tube inserted into the chest to remove air or fluid). On March 3, 2020, you had a pleurostomy (a surgical opening into the chest cavity). This opening was closed later. You then had a lung collapse again, which needed another pleural drainage (removing fluid from around the lung) and a Heimlich valve (a one-way valve attached to a chest drain) on March 10. The Heimlich valve was removed from the drain on March 27, but the drain was kept open for the pleurostomy. On March 31, you had a new pleurotomy (another surgical opening into the chest).

On April 7, you had an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (a surgery to open the chest to look inside) because of bleeding from tuberculous caverns (holes in the lung caused by TB). There was significant oozing bleeding. The cavity was packed with compresses (pads to stop bleeding). Post-surgery, on April 11, 2020, you had a right pneumonectomy (removal of your entire right lung) through a lateral thoracotomy (an incision on the side of your chest). You also had a tracheostomy (a surgical opening in the windpipe to help with breathing). Both the chest drain and the tracheostomy were removed on June 6.

You also developed surgical wound infections caused by a type of bacteria called Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, which is resistant to many antibiotics. This was treated with antibiotics: vancomycin, meropenem, and amikacin. This antibiotic treatment was stopped on April 2 after you showed improvement and a blood test called procalcitonin (which helps detect bacterial infection) showed a low value of 0.09.

On April 7, you experienced hypovolemic shock (a dangerous condition caused by severe blood loss) due to bleeding from the surgical wound of the pleurostomy, which required urgent surgery. Sadly, on April 10, you had a cardiopulmonary arrest (your heart and breathing stopped) for 4 minutes due to hypoxia (lack of oxygen), where your heart showed asystole (no electrical activity).

For your follow-up appointment, we have requested some tests. You will continue your TB treatment with RI (likely rifampin and isoniazid). We have given you prescriptions for 2 months. You will also continue taking oral iron replacement. We had a meeting with [person] and the thoracic surgery team to explain your condition and treatment and answer any questions. [person] understood the instructions and appreciated the care. We have scheduled follow-up appointments at [organization] and with the thoracic surgery team. We have told [person] about warning signs to look out for and instructed them to call if they have any concerns. We have provided a report and contacted [organization] for assisted treatment. Your care was managed by the infectious diseases and thoracic surgery teams. You are in good general condition and have no complaints.
